rows: Ground squirrels have two kinds of colour-sensing cells in their eyes, where people have three.

A golden-mantled ground squirrel can follow a light flickering at more than 100 times a second, and a yellow-pine chipmunk does about the same. An American red squirrel, a tree squirrel, stops following it at about 65, close to the 60 where a human stops. Nobody has measured a gray squirrel or a fox squirrel, so you very likely follow flicker at about the pace of the red squirrel.
A squirrel’s eyes sit on the sides of its head, which probably gives it a wide view with less detail than yours. This part of the view is a guess.

rows: If you are a California ground squirrel, your cones peak near 437 and 519 nanometers, one blue-sensitive and one green-sensitive. A gray squirrel's longer pigment peaks near 532, so the green end may sit a little further toward yellow for you.
Other ground squirrels have a blue cone near 436 nanometers and a green cone between 520 and 530. You very likely have the same pair, so reds and greens run together for you.

If you are a gray squirrel, the finest stripes you can tell apart in bright light are about 3.9 cycles per degree. A fox squirrel in dim light manages about 2.2, and a human reads about 30 on a chart.
You have no fovea. A red squirrel packs its cones densely in a horizontal streak below the optic nerve, and a California ground squirrel's streak has about five times as many cells as its edges.
A gray squirrel's dark-adapted sight peaks near 502 nanometers, the peak of a typical rod pigment. About four in ten of a gray squirrel's receptors are rod-like, and ground squirrels have far fewer.
An American red squirrel's eye follows flicker up to about 65 flashes a second in bright light. You very likely keep close to a human's pace.

A gray squirrel's lens holds a yellow pigment that removes short-wave light. In a thirteen-lined ground squirrel the lens absorbs everything below 410 nanometers, so almost no ultraviolet reaches your retina.

Nobody has measured how quickly your sharpness falls away from the streak, how strong your colors are, or the light levels at which rods take over from cones. Those settings are guesses, and so is the pupil, which is left round, and the width of your total field.
